newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM will push new law on Okinawa base leases.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM will push new law on Okinawa base leases.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Sunday said he aims to push through parliament a new law to ensure his government continues leases on private land used for key U.S. military bases on Okinawa.

Hashimoto's comments came on the day U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Tokyo. In a meeting with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, Gore said Washington had no plans to reduce troops on Okinawa, a thorny issue because of strong local opposition to the huge U.S. military presence.

"We will make our best efforts to make sure the government retains its rights (to lease) the pieces of land on Okinawa beyond the deadline," Hashimoto said in a speech at the graduation ceremony of the National Defence Academy.

Hashimoto faces a May 15 deadline on the expiration of his government's lease on land owned by 3,000 Okinawans covering 362,000 sq metres (433,000 sq yards) on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base.

His statement underlined his plans to seek parliamentary approval of an amendment to the current Special Land Expropriation Law, a revision which would enable his government to bypass lengthy land-lease processes and meet the deadline.
Private land used by the U.S. military is leased by the Japanese government, not the U.S. military itself.
Hashimoto's parliamentary allies, the Social Democratic Party and tiny New Party Sakigake, oppose the amendment, saying it would infuriate Okinawans.
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, an action Tokyo strongly opposes.
Okinawa is host to more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan, a legacy of the U.S. military occupation between the end of World War Two and 1972.
Hashimoto was scheduled to meet Gore on Monday. The Japanese prime minister is also to travel to Washington in late April for talks with President Bill Clinton.
